entries.title: Women's football in Germany booming but still much to do
entries.summary: Women's football is growing rapidly, particularly in Germany. Nevertheless, equal pay and investment remain major talking points.
entries.content:
September 18, 2026

Women's football is growing rapidly, particularly in Germany. Nevertheless, equal pay and investment remain major talking points.

According to the German Football Association (DFB), investment in women's football by professional clubs has risen by 135% over the past six years. In addition, the number of girls in Germany who play the game has increased by about 30% since 2022.

Celia Sasic, the former Germany striker who has been in charge of diversity and inclusion at the DFB since 2022, has helped bring women's football more into the spotlight in the boardroom.

"We've focused on the issue and established new structures, so that there is now a separate department with its own sports director," the 38-year-old told DW.

"In my view, it's important that there are very clear responsibilities for the development and professionalization of this sport."

"I believe it's important that [women's football] is recognized within the licensed clubs. And it's becoming increasingly recognized, so the framework conditions need to be adjusted," continued Sasic.

"And we're seeing that if we provide the right framework for the game, there's huge growth potential there."

Numbers support growth of women's game

The most-watched football match featuring a German team in 2025 was the Women's European Championship semifinal between Germany and Spain. The match drew around 14.26 million viewers—and a market share of about 57.6%. By comparison, the men's game against Portugal in the Nations League semifinals drew around 10 million viewers.

Sasic, who was part of the German team that won the 2009 and 2013 European championships, regards this as a foundation to build on.

"This is incredibly significant for us as a society and in terms of our influence abroad," she said.

"There are women who play football, who play for us on the national team, and who inspire us so much that millions of us watch their games."

'Zidane was my hero'

Sasic is clearly proud of the recent progress. For a long time, women's football in Germany was not taken seriously.

"I had no choice; I had to look to men for role models," Sasic recalled.

"My biggest role model was Zinedine Zidane. I had posters of [Luis] Figo, [David] Beckham, and Michael Ballack hanging in my room."

Posters of women wouldn't have existed back then, but it's different now. These days, Germany captain Giulia Gwinn and players like Jule Brandt and Lea Schüller smile down from the walls of children's bedrooms, inspiring girls to dream of a great career in women's football.

Further investment required to push women's game forward

Despite the boom, the financial gap between women's and men's football remains enormous, as figures from the DFB and the German Soccer League (DFL) show. While the 18 Bundesliga clubs spent €1.72 billion ($1.9 billion) on players and coaching staff alone in the 2024–25 season, the personnel expenses of the 12 Women's Bundesliga clubs most recently totaled just under €30 million — about 60 times lower.

Salaries also highlight how the professionalization of women's football is still very much in its infancy. In the 2023-24 season, a women's Bundesliga player earned an average base salary of around €48,000 per year. Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane is estimated to have earned €25 million during the same season.

This disparity is expected to narrow in the future.

"Football reflects our society—and thus also the gender inequality and the gender pay gap that we see in our society," former German Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock told DW.

"Unfortunately, this gap in football is even wider in many countries than in other professions. But that is by no means set in stone," added Baerbock, who also served as the president of the United Nations General Assembly from September 2025 to September 2026.

"We know from the USA, the United Kingdom, Norway, and Spain that if you really want to invest in women's football, equal pay is an important part of that—especially when it comes to tournament bonuses."

Young women need professional support

Celia Sasic currently sees significant progress when it comes to women's football, although it's still early days in the development process.

"Clubs must provide all the necessary resources to enable this development. Football pitches, medical care, a fitness facility, and a coaching staff must be available," said Sasic. "Investing in this ultimately makes the game much better, too."

Opportunities for young girls in terms of training also need to improve.

"It's a crucial step to have youth development centers where players are trained—not only athletically, but also professionally. These are essential factors for the success of the women's game."

Education and apprenticeship options must be available

A new DFB rule shows that even basic professional structures still need to be established. Only since the 2025–26 season have teams in the Women's Bundesliga been required to employ assistant coaches, goalkeeper coaches, and athletic coaches on a full-time, professional basis.

Sasic and women's football still have a long way to go, but the former player is determined to continue fighting for greater equality. The 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil is a great place to start, and Sasic is hoping for a successful showing for Germany at the tournament as this would likely give women's football another major boost—and bring broadcasters new record viewership ratings.

This article was adapted from German.

entries.title: Bolivia: New cat species discovered by scientists
entries.summary: Genetic data confirmed that the small feline, called "tilcayo" by locals, is a new species of cat. It's the first such discovery in more than 100 years.
entries.content:
September 18, 2026

Genetic data confirmed that the small feline, called "tilcayo" by locals, is a new species of cat. It's the first such discovery in more than 100 years.

Scientists in Bolivia have identified a small wild cat with a leopard-like coat as a previously unknown species.

Local communities call the feline "tilcayo," a nickname that inspired the cat's new scientific designation: Leopardus tilcayo.

Biologist and National Geographic explorer Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz described the discovery as a "remarkable event, because a new wild cat species hasn't been described in 100 years."

The last feline species to be discovered was the Uruguayan pampas cat in 1923.

What do we know about Leopardus tilcayo?

The cat was found in Bolivia's Yungas forest, a remote region on the eastern slope of the Andes mountains.

The animal measures around 18 inches (46 centimeters) long and weighs around 3 pounds (1.4 kilograms), making it smaller than the average domestic cat.

"Its fur is light brown ... with irregularly shaped rosettes across its body," Nogales-Ascarrunz said.

According to National Geographic, Nogales-Ascarrunz first came upon the animal in 2016 after receiving a call from a local wildlife sanctuary.

The organization said at the time that it had been handed "a weird cat."

"I took a hundred pictures of it," Nogales-Ascarrunz told National Geographic. "I was so fascinated."

It was a few years later that she realized the cat she had photographed was unlike any previously seen.

Species finds its place in cat family tree

Research on the new species was published this week in the journal Current Biology.

Using genetic analysis in collaboration with geneticist Eduardo Eizirik, co-lead authors Nogales-Ascarrunz and the University of Antwerp's Jonas Lescroart were able to place the feline in its specific category in the cat family tree.

Nogales-Ascarrunz said that a pair of tilcayos have undergone whole-genome sequencing and are the only such creatures found so far.

"So far, it's only been detected in Bolivia" and not "anywhere else on the planet," Nogales-Ascarrunz said.

"Showing the general public that even in a flagship group such as cats ... there are still new species to be discovered may transmit an important message," said Eizirik, who is an evolutionary biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil.

"There are many undiscovered species out there in the world, and they are at risk of disappearing before we even discover them."

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: India news: Long queues hit stores as new iPhones go on sale
entries.summary: The iPhone 18 has gone on sale in India, drawing huge queues across the country. Meanwhile, the Election Commission has barred both Trinamool factions from using the party's name in by-elections. Follow DW for more.
entries.content:
India

India news: Long queues hit stores as new iPhones go on sale

Published September 18, 2026last updated September 18, 2026

The iPhone 18 has gone on sale in India, drawing huge queues across the country. Meanwhile, the Election Commission has barred both Trinamool factions from using the party's name in by-elections. Follow DW for more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • The new iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max have hit the Indian markets, leading to long queues outside stores
  • The Election Commission has barred both factions of the Trinamool Congress from using the party name and symbol in upcoming bypolls
  • Cricket's global governing body is eyeing new viewership, this time from China

Here is a roundup of some of the top headlines from across India on Friday, September 18:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section READ — Smuggling suspected as more rare animals seen in India

READ — Smuggling suspected as more rare animals seen in India

Five infant orangutans, a species found only on the Indonesian island of Sumatra and on Borneo, were found in a forest by rangers patrolling in the Balasore district of India's eastern Odisha state last week.

In recent years, orangutans, rare reptiles and other exotic animals are popping up in India, suggesting the country is becoming a major destination for trafficked wildlife.

Skip next section iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max go on sale in India, prompting long queues

iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max go on sale in India, prompting long queues

Long lines formed outside Apple Stores across India on Friday as the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max went on sale — this year's most expensive Pro lineup to date, with prices roughly Rs 30,000 (€270, $310) higher than last year's equivalent models at launch.

The high prices were not a barrier for many buyers, whose wait began before dawn. In Bengaluru, a customer named Rahul told newswire ANI he arrived at the Apple Store around 5 a.m. local time and found people already in line.

Rahul, who said he has bought every iPhone since the iPhone 7, described the ritual as something bigger than a purchase: "I've been purchasing iPhones for a very long time ... But it's like a festival for me. iPhone launch is like a festival. Every year, I try to buy an iPhone."

At the Apple Store in the northern city of Noida, one buyer said he had traveled from the nearby state of Punjab and began his wait at 6 a.m. local time, just to be first through the door: "Mine was the very first booking; I am the first one who has got the phone."

This year's price increase — pushing the iPhone 18 Pro to Rs 164,900 (€1,500, $1,720) and the Pro Max to Rs 179,900 (€1,635, $1,900) at the base storage tier — breaks Apple's recent run of holding launch prices steady in India.

India's GDP per capita stood at $2,702.5 in 2025, according to World Bank figures. The numbers do not account for income inequality.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Seerat at DW's Studio Delhi, starting the day off on a relatively peaceful note, about 6 kilometers (four miles) from all the madness (read: the Apple store on launch day).

Long queues snaked around Apple stores across the country as the new iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max hit the market in India. These might be some of the most expensive phones in history, but that hasn't deterred die-hard fans.

Meanwhile, in a move that opposition leaders have dubbed the Election Commission of India's "late night birthday gift to Modi ji," the electoral body has barred both factions of the Trinamool Congress from using the name "All India Trinamool Congress" and its symbol, flowers and grass, ahead of upcoming bypolls.

Finally, if 1.4 billion Indians were not enough, the International Cricket Council (ICC) is seeking to create a new fanbase by tapping into Chinese potential.

For this and more, follow our live blog.

entries.title: Philippines: At least 2 students killed in school shooting
entries.summary: Emergency services received reports of gunfire at the Banga National High School in southern Mindanao on Friday afternoon. At least two students were killed, while several others were injured.
entries.content:
Philippines

Philippines: At least 2 students killed in school shooting

September 18, 2026

Emergency services received reports of gunfire at the Banga National High School in southern Mindanao on Friday afternoon. At least two students were killed, while several others were injured.

At least three people have been killed, including the suspected gunman, at a school shooting incident in the southern Philippines on Friday, officials said. Several other wounded students have been taken to the hospital.

"The incident resulted in three confirmed deaths and several individuals wounded," Philippine National Police said in a statement.

What we know

Emergency services were called to Banga National High School in South Cotabato province in Mindanao at about 1:30 p.m. local time (0530 GMT).

South Cotabato Governor Reynaldo Tamayo said two students were killed, a boy and a girl, both 14, and that the gunman was the third person who died.

Banga town mayor ​Albert Palencia ⁠was quoted by the Reuters news agency as saying that the third person, believed to be a 16-year-old suspected gunman, was also killed.

Eight people were injured, with four in citical condition, he said, adding that the victims were all aged between 14 and 17.

Incident under investigation

"The incident remains under investigation. Responding police personnel immediately secured the area and coordinated with school authorities and medical responders to assist those affected and ensure the safety of students and school personnel," police said.

It was not immediately clear how many shooters were involved.

There was also no immediate information about a possible motive.

In a video posted on Facebook and verified by the AFP news agency, a man is seen carrying what appears to be a wounded child from the school.

In another, a teacher speaking in a local dialect can be heard saying there were two shooters, with a student insisting they were outsiders.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Everything you need to know about Oktoberfest 2026
entries.summary: This year, AI will be used to manage overcrowded situations. Find all the numbers surrounding the fest — including the price of water!
entries.content:
September 18, 2026

This year, AI will be used to manage overcrowded situations. Find all the numbers surrounding the fest — including the price of water!

On Saturday, September 19, at noon, Oktoberfest will once again open with the ceremonial tapping of the keg, during which the mayor of Munich drives a tap into the first wooden barrel of beer and calls out "O'zapft is," a Bavarian phrase that translates to "It's tapped."

His call will be followed by 12 gunshots, a signal that lets all festival tents know that they can start serving beer.

More than 6 million people are expected at the world's largest Volksfest, which runs this year through October 4.

Expanded security measures to prevent overcrowding

The festival grounds are enormous: Oktoberfest takes place on Munich's Theresienwiese, a 34.5-hectare site roughly the size of 48 soccer fields.

But crowds can swell, especially on weekends — sometimes to dangerous levels.

Last year, officials had to temporarily close the entrances.

One reason is that nearly all 38 beer tents operate in two or three reservation shifts. When one group of guests leaves and the next arrives at the 14 large tents — which each accommodate several thousand people — huge numbers of visitors end up trying to enter and exit at the same time.

That's how, on one Saturday afternoon at last year's Oktoberfest, the crowds became so dense that movement temporarily came to a standstill. The crush caused some visitors to panic.

To prevent that from happening again, the city of Munich has overhauled its security plan for this year's festival.

Twenty-six new cameras, in addition to 56 police cameras, will monitor the grounds, while an AI system will analyze visitor flows and issue alerts if areas become overcrowded.

A newly established coordination center is also intended to improve communication between security agencies and event organizers.

Organizers and police have also drawn up a plan to defend against drones over the grounds, though no details have been disclosed.

In addition, 600 police officers will be deployed on site.

Oktoberfest is famous worldwide, but most visitors are local

Oktoberfest may be known around the world as an international tourist attraction, but most of its visitors don't travel very far to get there.

A study commissioned by the city of Munich last year found that the festival remains overwhelmingly regional.

In 2025, 41% of visitors came from Munich, another 25% from the surrounding area and 9% from elsewhere in the region. In all, three-quarters of Oktoberfest's roughly 6.5 million visitors came from Bavaria. Another 4% came from elsewhere in Germany.

About 21% of visitors — roughly 1.35 million people — traveled from abroad. Americans made up the largest group of international visitors, accounting for just under 20% of the total, or more than 270,000 people. Italians were next, at just over 13%.

Beer prices rise again

Cannabis is banned throughout the festival grounds.

Alcohol, on the other hand, is available in whatever quantities visitors are willing — and able — to pay for. A Mass, the traditional 1-liter mug of beer served at Oktoberfest, costs between €14.80 and €15.90 ($17-$18.25) this year, only slightly more than last year.

A liter of table water comes in at a hefty €11, although the grounds also have several free drinking water fountains.

Visitors planning to enjoy one of Oktoberfest's many rides would be wise to stay relatively sober. Tickets cost anywhere from just under €5 to €14.

Germany's traditional fairground culture was officially added to the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2026, and that tradition remains very much alive at the 191st Oktoberfest. According to organizers, about 90% of the festival's more than 130 fairground operators trace their roots back to the 19th century.

The festival remains decidedly traditional when it comes to payment, too: Many vendors still accept cash only. Visitors caught without any can withdraw money from ATMs on the grounds.

Dirndl or lederhosen for Oktoberfest?

Then there's the question of what to wear.

Bavarians who take pride in doing things properly generally show up in local traditional dress.

The dirndl is the traditional dress worn by women and girls, which consists of close-fitting bodice with a low neckline, a blouse worn under the bodice, a wide high-waisted skirt and an apron.

Men wear lederhosen, the traditional leather shorts or knee-length breeches with suspenders.

For those who are not Bavarian, lederhosen and dirndls are certainly an option, but they're by no means required. Munich's event marketing department, Simply Munich, advises first-time visitors to consider renting traditional garb rather than buying it.

Be aware that locals find cheap imitations of traditional dress off-putting, as Simply Munich points out: "If you want to avoid wry looks, steer clear of Seppl hats, 'leather pants' made of cloth and garish mini plastic dirndls. With jeans and a checkered shirt, you'll definitely be more suitably dressed."

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Australia: Man killed in shark attack near Perth
entries.summary: A swimmer was mauled by a shark, with witnesses reporting a massive pool of blood in the water. There have been four confirmed fatal shark attacks in Australia this year.
entries.content:
Australia

Australia: Man killed in shark attack near Perth

September 18, 2026

A swimmer was mauled by a shark, with witnesses reporting a massive pool of blood in the water. There have been four confirmed fatal shark attacks in Australia this year.

A swimmer off the coast of Perth in Western Australia was killed by a shark on Friday, police said.

Emergency services were called to Sorrento Beach in the north of the city to search for the man. Earlier, witnesses said they had watched the man being attacked by a shark, with blood pooling in the water, Australian media reported.

It is unclear whether any remains were recovered, and no details of the victim's identity have yet been shared.

"It was reported a male swimmer had been bitten by a shark while swimming along the coast," a Western Australia state police spokeswoman said in a statement.

"The swimmer died as a result of the attack."

The beach was closed following the attack.

Several killed this year by sharks

Friday's incident would be the fifth fatal shark attack in Australia this year. Previously, there were four confirmed fatal shark attacks.

In May and June, three spearfishing divers were killed by sharks in seperate incidents. In January, a 12-year-old boy died in hospital after being mauled by a bull shark in Sydney Harbor.

On Monday, a surfer was severely wounded in the leg near the city of Geraldton, 400 kilometers (250 miles) north of Perth on Australia's west coast.

Over the past 25 years, Australia has averaged between two and three fatal shark attacks annually, according to the Australian Shark Incident Database.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Venezuela unblocks some news websites censored for years
entries.summary: Venezuela has restored access to 17 news sites that were blocked for years under Nicolas Maduro's administration. While activists welcomed the move, they noted that dozens more news portals, remain inaccessible.
entries.content:
September 18, 2026

Venezuela has restored access to 17 news sites that were blocked for years under Nicolas Maduro's administration. While activists welcomed the move, they noted that dozens more news portals, remain inaccessible.

Venezuela has lifted restrictions on several news websites that had been censored for years, its telecom regulator said.

Under the administration of Nicolas Maduro, who was captured by the US in January, hundreds of national and international websites, as well as various news portals, were censored.

Following Maduro's ouster, Washington has backed talks between the interim government, led by Delcy Rodriguez, and parts of the opposition. The decision to unblock the websites came ahead of the second round of talks in Caracas. 

Dinorah Figuera, head of the opposition delegation in the talks, celebrated the decision in a post on X.

"Informing without fear cannot continue to be a privilege, but must be compliance with the law. This is a first step; there are still many media outlets missing, and they all have to return," she said.

Dozens of sites still blocked

VE Sin Filtro, a digital rights organization, confirmed that 17 news sites had been unblocked and that they were accessible through different internet providers. It added that 188 websites remain inaccessible, including 79 news portals.

Journalists and NGOs have long denounced the censorship imposed under Maduro.

Some users relied on VPNs to access these websites.

Deputy Communications Minister Gustavo Villapol said the decision was aimed at ending polarization.

"We can never again vilify people without having proof in hand; we cannot use communication for interests that are external to the vital meaning of our nation," he said on state television.

Journalists respond with skepticism

Luis Ernesto Blanco, editorial director of Runrunes, one of the unblocked websites, said Thursday's move amounted to an official acknowledgment that public debate had been stifled.

Victor Amaya, who runs the TalCual news portal blocked in mid-2024, voiced skepticism that all censored sites would become accessible again, but said he hoped the change would lead to "a normalized communication environment."

The TalCual portal lost 60% of its audience due to the blockade, as well as much of its advertising revenue.

Media watchdog Reporters Without Borders last month said repression, censorship, restricted access to information and an increasingly hostile legal environment had severely stifled independent journalism in Venezuela.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Malaysia: Jailed ex-leader Najib allowed house arrest
entries.summary: Convicted in the 1MDB scandal for embezzling millions, former Prime Minister Najib Razak had repeatedly sought clemency. Malaysia's king has now granted him a "conditional pardon."
entries.content:
September 18, 2026

Convicted in the 1MDB scandal for embezzling millions, former Prime Minister Najib Razak had repeatedly sought clemency. Malaysia's king has now granted him a "conditional pardon."

Malaysia's graft-convicted former Prime Minister Najib Razak was granted royal clemency and will be allowed to sit out the remainder of a six-year jail term in house arrest, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim's legal department said on Friday.

King Sultan Ibrahim "has granted a conditional pardon" to Najib, "allowing him to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest" until August 23, 2028," lawyers said.

The conditional pardon is subject to the payment of 50 million Malaysian ringgit ($12.3 million; €10.7 million).

Billions stolen from state funds

Najib, 73, is currently serving a six-year term in prison for his role in the 1MDB corruption scandal, named after 1Malaysia Development Berhad, a state investment fund he co-founded while serving as prime minister from 2009 to 2018.

In 2020, Najib was originally sentenced to 12 years in prison for abuse of power, criminal breach of trust and money laundering involving $10.3 million funneled into his bank accounts. He began his sentence in 2022.

In a separate case, Najib was convicted in December 2025 of abuse of power and money laundering, accused of misappropriating nearly $569 million from 1MDB. He was fined $2.8 billion and sentenced to another 15 years in prison, which is to take effect after his existing sentence ends. He is currently appealing that conviction.

It was not specified on Friday whether the clemency applied to the first conviction affects the second case.

Royal clemency and the law

It is not the first time Najib has received a pardon. Under the previous king in 2024, Najib saw the sentence from his first conviction of 12 years cut in half, and fines reduced. At the time, he had sought unsuccessfully to secure house arrest.

Najib's ⁠legal ​team has not yet commented on Friday's decision, and it is not immediately clear when the former leader will be released into house arrest.

Investigators allege the 1MDB scandal involved at least $4.5 billion in state funds that were stolen and laundered by top executives and associates of Najib. Najib has always denied wrongdoing and has tried to frame himself as a scapegoat.

The embezzlement scandal sparked national outrage in Malaysia and led to the 2018 election defeat of Najib's party United Malays National Organization (UNMO), which had governed the country since independence from Britain in 1957.

The scion of a prominent political family, Najib was long seen as untouchable. He still holds political clout in Malaysia, and Friday's royal clemency could lead to questions over equal treatment under the law.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: VAR's mission creep a problem for football
entries.summary: After a decade of use, questions around VAR in football are louder than ever. Has the technology strayed too far from its remit?
entries.content:
SportsGlobal issues

VAR's mission creep a problem for football

September 18, 2026

After a decade of use, questions around VAR in football are louder than ever. Has the technology strayed too far from its remit?

Another domestic football season is underway and already, in mid-September, the shortcomings of technology in sport are at the center of the discourse once again.

The video assistant referee (VAR) is perhaps the most discussed technology in modern sport. While video replays have been in use for years in sports like American football, rugby or cricket, it has only been a decade since the International Football Association Board (IFAB), the highest regulatory authority in the sport, approved the use of VAR.

With artificial intelligence (AI) reportedly reaching dangerous levels of development and technological optimization of people's lives at an all-time high, it is perhaps a pertinent time to consider the use of technology in sport. Has it finally evolved from a supporting role to an all-powerful, game-altering one?

"The idea behind VAR was that technology could reduce human error while leaving the referee in charge," Susmit Gulavani, an assistant professor in AI and machine learning in sport at the University of South Carolina, told DW.

"Over time, however, VAR has expanded in both its use and its influence. The introduction of newer technologies, such as AI-assisted Semi-Automated Offside Technology (SAOT), has made it an increasingly central part of decision making. While these advances have improved the precision of offside decisions, they have also raised expectations that technology should deliver perfect outcomes," he said.

"That is where the sense of "mission creep" comes from. VAR is now expected to resolve almost every contentious decision, even though many incidents, such as fouls or handball decisions, still require human interpretation."

That pursuit of perfection often leaves fans waiting and confused, and it breaks up a game that is fast and fluid. The World Cup this summer was evidence of that. And yet, if anything, the technology looks like it is finding more ways to embed itself into the sport.

VAR in the Bundesliga under the spotlight

It has been nine years since VAR was introduced to the Bundesliga.

After the World Cup, German officials confirmed that VAR will also be allowed to have a say in second yellow cards and corner kicks in the Bundesliga. Granting technology additional powers did not go down well with organized fan groups in the country though, who launched a coordinated campaign calling for VAR to be scrapped in August this year. The broad message was that the technology has "robbed football of its joy" and that it was time to put the cameras back in the box.

This is particularly significant in Germany, where many fans are club members and therefore have genuine influence over the actions of their club and the governance of the game. Jochen Drees, the head of VAR operations in Germany, has however argued for refining the technology rather than removing it – a natural tendency, according to Gulavani.

VAR mission creep a symbol of technology's power

"VAR is a useful example of a broader societal pattern. As technology becomes more capable, we increasingly rely on it, but we also have to decide where its role should begin and end," he said.

"The appeal is understandable because AI can significantly improve efficiency and productivity. Tasks that once took hours can often be completed in minutes. At the same time, this expansion raises important questions about privacy, transparency, accountability, environmental costs, and where human judgment should remain central."

What will technology in sport look like in the future?

Sport without this technology is unlikely. Business, recruitment and event management are already finding ways to be more efficient thanks to the introduction of AI and other technologies.

As for VAR, perhaps a different system is required. At the U20 men's football World Cup last year, challenge cards, as seen in the NFL for example, were trialed. Coaches could ask for situations to be reviewed, reducing the interference of constant replays and slow-motion assessments. Reportedly, trialing of the approach, officially called Football Video Support (FVS), continues but it is likely seen as a cheaper alternative to the expensive VAR rather than a replacement.

"The key is to treat technology as decision support rather than decision replacement," Gulavani said. "

AI and technologies like VAR are good at processing large amounts of information quickly and consistently, but they cannot fully understand the context, intent, or nuance that many sporting decisions require. Human referees are still needed to interpret the Laws of the Game and exercise judgment in situations where there is no objectively 'correct' answer."

A return to a previous era seems unlikely, but the challenge is familiar. Can sport find a way to return technology to a supporting role rather than one that governs it to such an extent that it removes human engagement and emotion? If it can, perhaps those ripples will be felt beyond the white lines of sporting arenas.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

entries.title: Organized crime and drug-related deaths rise Germany
entries.summary: Presenting its annual report for organized crime, the German police said that cocaine was a danger for the state and society, and that the cases of money laundering had increased.
entries.content:
September 18, 2026

Presenting its annual report for organized crime, the German police said that cocaine was a danger for the state and society, and that the cases of money laundering had increased.

"We are experiencing a flood of cocaine in Germany," German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, from the Christian Democrats (CDU), said earlier this week as a new police report was presented. "We are experiencing a record number of drug-related deaths. We are seeing children being exploited as criminals."

Standing alongside Dobrindt, Holger Münch, the president of the Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), and Hendrik Streeck, the German government's drug and addiction commissioner, presented findings described as alarming.

Last year, 10 tons of cocaine were seized, two thirds of that amount in German ports. And 2,150 people lost their lives because of drug use, 13 more than in 2024.

Profits generated from drugs by international organized crime networks are often invested in real estate to conceal their origin. Münch said that 195 cases of money laundering, amounting to almost €1.4 billion (ca. $1.6 billion) had been investigated in 2025.

"They [the criminals] use their considerable financial clout to bribe and to exert influence," he said. "And they launder the money and funnel it into the legal economic system."

He added that the most widely used drug was cocaine and that it posed a threat to the state, the economy and society as a whole.

'There is blood on every gram of cocaine consumed for pleasure'

"It is not only the state that is being damaged," said Streeck. "Above all, it is people who are being damaged."

About 83% of the drug-related deaths concerned men, whose average age was 41.

"They are all customers of a market that deals in deadly substances and is driven by violence, environmental destruction, extortion and exploitation," said Streeck, who trained as a doctor.

He insisted that there should be zero tolerance for those who profited from addiction and zero indifference to those suffering from it. His focus is on preventative measures, which include a public awareness campaign about the impact on health and the environment.

He explained that in some countries, rainforests were being cleared to make way for cocaine production. Streek pointed out that toxic substances used for processing the drug, such as kerosene or battery acid, ended up in the soil and water. Farmers and their families were blackmailed. He lamented the fact that cocaine had become more popular in Germany. 

"There is blood on every gram of cocaine consumed for pleasure," the drug and addiction commissioner stated.

Digitalization of drugs trade

Streeck added that the situation had changed significantly in recent years and the market had gone digital.

"Dealers are no longer on the street corner; they're on the phone. For example, people can order so-called 'cocaine taxis' [cars that deliver drugs to any location] via QR code," he said.

"What is particularly alarming is that criminal groups are recruiting minors through social media or gaming platforms," he added. "Organized criminals look for recruits in the places where young people spend their free time."

Münch noted that this development posed a particular challenge for German and international law enforcement agencies. He said that, more and more, the cliched image of organized crime — discretion, isolation and closed structures — was a thing of the past. The fact that people can purchase criminal services on the dark web represents a paradigm shift, according to Münch: "It's not just a question of who commits a crime, but of who ordered it, who financed it, who is profiting from it?"

Moreover, there is a suspicion on the part of investigators that state actors are increasingly involved in opaque crime activities, launching attacks as "hybrid threats."

Münch said that "money laundering, corruption and violence can contribute to social destabilization." 

In 2025, there were about 600 investigations into cases of organized crime in Germany, which has been the average for the past five years. The German police considers one of its major successes to be the shutdown of the Archetyp Market, an online drug marketplace on the darknet. Its administrator was arrested in June 2025. He had overseen the sale of cocaine, heroin, cannabis and other drugs, amounting to 250 million. When the platform was shut down there were 3,200 registered sellers and 612,000 customer accounts according to the police.
